claims.text: Allen characterises Pico as an Aristotelian by training and an eclectic by conviction, not a devout Neoplatonist like Ficino.

quotes.text: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463-94) was the wunderkind among Italian Renaissance philosophers and a key figure, along with Cusanus, Bessarion, and Ficino, in the revival of Platonic metaphysics, though he was not a devout Neoplatonist like Ficino but rather an Aristotelian by training and in many ways an eclectic by conviction.

bears_on.note: Contrasts Pico's eclecticism with Ficino's Neoplatonic commitment.

claims.text: Allen reports that Pico sent a draft of the Commento to Ficino, who found off-the-cuff attacks on his own views and wrote marginalia on it before returning it.

quotes.text: Pico also sent a draft to Ficino, presumably for his reactions. In working through it, however, Ficino found several off-the-cuff attacks on his own views, either aimed at him directly or at "a distinguished Platonist" who was wrong on such and such an issue (clearly himself), and he was agitated enough to pen his own marginalia, with abrupt remarks such as "This is a bad mistake," before sending the draft back to Pico.

bears_on.note: Ficino's marginalia on Pico's draft; the Commento is the locus of the quarrel.

judged.justification: Refines the picture of the Ficino-Pico exchange by tying it to the Commento draft.

claims.text: Allen holds that the disagreement over the Commento did not become a feud or estrangement, though Pico took only partial account of Ficino's corrections.

quotes.text: Nonetheless, this scholarly contention did not develop, as it well might have, into an academic feud or estrangement, even though Pico, in revising and reorganizing, took only partial, one might even say high-handed, account of Ficino's corrections, incorporating some of them and rebutting others

bears_on.note: The quarrel over the Commento stayed scholarly, not personal, on Allen's reading.

claims.text: Allen reports that Pico asserted at the end of Commento 2.2 that Marsilio had made mistakes on every subject in every part of his De amore.

quotes.text: asseverated at the end of 2.2 that Marsilio had "made mistakes on every subject in every part of his treatise [i.e., the De amore]."

bears_on.note: Pico's sweeping charge against Ficino's De amore, as reported by Allen.

claims.text: Allen infers that Benivieni, Gianfrancesco and friends concealed Pico's disagreements with Ficino, and that Benivieni's expurgated version omitted the references to Ficino.

quotes.text: Benivieni too deliberately suppressed Pico's original version and eventually reorganized, expanded, and in places completely rewrote an expurgated version that omitted the references to Ficino and was stylistically and in other aspects much more polished.

It seems that, like Gianfrancesco, he and other friends were anxious to conceal the disagreements with Ficino, lest these disagreements and indeed the relationship between the two luminaries be misunderstood.

bears_on.note: Later editors concealed the Pico-Ficino disagreements in the Commento's transmission.
Benivieni's expurgated rewrite of the Commento.

claims.text: Allen reports that Ficino regarded the Commento notes as full of youthful errors whose publication would not enhance Pico's reputation, citing a letter to Ganay.

quotes.text: Moreover, since Ficino himself certainly considered the notes replete with youthful errors whose publication would not enhance Pico's reputation, as he had observed in a letter to Germain de Ganay in Paris dated March 23, 1495

bears_on.note: Ficino's own judgement of the Commento after Pico's death.

claims.text: Allen says the Commento does not always persuade in Pico's disputes with Ficino, and that its combative style belongs to the conventions of Renaissance scholarly disagreement.

quotes.text: The work hardly compares to Ficino's De amore, either in length or breadth, though it raises a number of subtle points and has a rapid-fire brilliance to it. Nor indeed does it always persuade us that Pico is right in his series of contretemps with Ficino, and its combative mode of arguing has to be understood in the light of the conventions of Renaissance scholarly disagreements

bears_on.note: Allen's assessment of the Commento's contretemps with Ficino.

claims.text: Allen says that when writing the Commento Pico was not yet well acquainted with the Phaedrus and Hermias's commentary on it, the Charmides, or sections of the Enneads.

quotes.text: More surprisingly, Pico is not (yet) well acquainted with Platonic texts that have a bearing on the Symposium, especially the Phaedrus, along with Hermias's commentary on it; the Charmides; and various sections of the Enneads.

judged.justification: Qualifies how much direct Proclean/Hermian reading can be assumed behind the Commento.

claims.text: Allen says the real concern of the Commento is metaphysics, conceived as a dimension of theology and read in Greco-Roman myth and less in Egyptian and Chaldean myth, rather than love theory.

quotes.text: And despite his protestations, he is not concerned with love theory except in a rudimentary form. What does concern him is metaphysics (which he thinks of as a dimension of theology), especially metaphysics as he sees it embedded in Greco-Roman myth and to a lesser extent in the myths of Egypt and the Chaldean Oracles

claims.text: Allen presents Pico's ecstasy as two deaths: in the first the soul's lower powers cease but the intellect gazes on the heavenly Venus, in the second the body falls away and the soul unites with her in a kiss.

quotes.text: In the amatory ecstasy or frenzy ... the soul separates from the body in the sense that all its lower powers cease to function, but with one exception: the nutritive or vegetative soul continues in a subdued or minimal way to maintain the body's life. Otherwise the soul's intellect is supremely active and gazes upon the heavenly Venus, the Idea of Beauty

If, however, the activity of the intellect becomes so sovereign that it no longer stops at all, then the body falls totally away from the soul, and the soul joins with the heavenly Venus "in an intimate embrace" that is perfected in the union of the kiss, the two becoming "a single soul."

judged.justification: Allen's account of the first and second death frames the kiss as angelic transformation.

claims.text: Allen reports Pico saying that Cabalist wise men held many ancient fathers to have died in intellectual rapture, and that the Cabalists call this death binsica, death from kissing.

quotes.text: Since the Cabalist wise men believe that many of the ancient fathers died in this kind of rapture of the intellect, you will find the Cabalists saying that those fathers died of binsica which in our language means death from kissing," and he lists Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, Aaron, and Mary (i.e., Miriam).

claims.text: Allen reports that Pico says Solomon longs for the death of the kiss in a verse of Canticles, and Plato too in speaking of the kisses of Agathon.

quotes.text: The death from kissing occurs "when the soul in intellectual rapture unites so completely with incorporeal things that it rises above the body and leaves it altogether." Solomon longs for such an amatory death, says Pico, in the verse "Kiss me with the kisses of thy mouth" (Canticles 1:2), and Plato too when he speaks of the kisses of Agathon.

pico_locus.ref: gloss on Da lui el foco

claims.text: Allen holds that for Pico union with intelligible Beauty means passing from human to intellectual existence and being transformed into an angel, as the Cabalists say Enoch became Metatron.

quotes.text: Or has he now forgotten Orpheus and been swept up by the idea of a total union with intelligible Beauty that cannot be obtained while we are sensible beings? But such a union means, as he had intimated earlier in glossing this same lemma, Da lui el foco, that we pass "from human existence to intellectual existence" and are by that death transformed into an angel, as the Cabalists declare Enoch was transformed into Metatron, "the angel of divinity."

judged.justification: Ties the Death of the Kiss to the Enoch-Metatron transformation in the Commento.

claims.text: Allen says that through the kiss-death we cease to be human and become angels, the cherubim and seraphim of Ezekiel's vision.

quotes.text: To attain such a gift, the soul separates from the body, but, even more importantly, the body drops away entirely from the soul. We cease to be humans and become angels - the cherubim and seraphim of Ezekiel's great vision.

claims.text: Allen finds it unclear whether Pico means Orpheus should have died the second death or only the first, and asks whether he has thought the situation through.

quotes.text: But has he really thought the situation through? Is he saying in effect that Orpheus should have died the second death, that Orpheus should have been a Jacob or a Moses? Or simply that he should have died the first death, that is, fled to Eurydice in intellectual rapture while his body remained alive

open_questions.text: Whether Pico intends the first or the second death for Orpheus is left open.

basis_quote.text: But has he really thought the situation through?

pico_locus.ref: gloss on Per lui el fonte immortale

claims.text: Allen reports that Pico says God does not love us because love in God would be an imperfection, and reads this as aimed at Ficino, who held that God loves us.

quotes.text: he emphasizes that the soul's ecstatic intellectual vision, which is transcendent love of God, is not reciprocated by God; God, he says, ... does not love us, because such a love in God "would be an imperfection" in him.
His intention at this point seems to be to shock the reader, or at least to refute Ficino, who is specifically cited as believing, incorrectly, that God loves us

bears_on.note: Pico's denial that God loves us is directed at Ficino's doctrine of reciprocation.

judged.justification: Identifies a concrete doctrinal target of Pico's anti-Ficinian polemic.

pico_locus.ref: gloss on Che poi che in se

claims.text: Allen reports that Pico denies there is beauty in God, according to the Platonists, because of infinite simplicity, so God must be loved in himself and not as author of ideal beauty.

quotes.text: the arresting argument that "there is no beauty in God, according to the Platonists, because of his infinite simplicity," beauty having been previously defined as an ordering of parts into a whole. Rather, says Pico, we can only love God "in Himself" and not "as the author of ideal beauty."

claims.text: Allen says Pico's Commento presents Platonic psychology keyed to being rather than, as in Ficino, to unity, though Pico is indebted to the third book of Ficino's Platonic Theology.

quotes.text: So let us turn now to Pico's presentation of Platonic psychology in the Commento, which is keyed, interestingly, to being and not, as in Ficino, to unity - though we should note that Pico is clearly indebted to the third book of Ficino's Platonic Theology and its exploration of God's attributes, including God's role in our understanding.

bears_on.note: Contrast: Pico keys the Commento to being, Ficino to unity.
Pico is indebted to Platonic Theology III.

judged.justification: Places the being/unity split, later central to De ente et uno, already in the Commento.

claims.text: Allen says the Commento begins by distinguishing causal, formal and participated being, defining God as cause of being and of all intellect rather than as being or intellect per se.

quotes.text: The Commento begins with an ontological preoccupation by distinguishing among causal, formal, and participated being as a fundamental Platonic ... postulate and by defining God not as being per se but as the cause of being and not as an intellect per se but as the source and cause of all intellect.

claims.text: Allen reports that Pico challenges a great Platonist's amazement at Plotinus's saying that God understands nothing, explaining that understanding exists in God in causal, not formal, being.

quotes.text: This leads Pico from the onset to challenge the reaction of amazement by "un gran platonico" (clearly Ficino) to a passage in Plotinus's Enneads (5.6.3 or 6.7.37) in which God is said to understand nothing and to castigate him for not realizing that Plotinus merely intended that "the attribute of understanding exists in God in its causal not formal being

bears_on.note: Pico's opening polemic against Ficino's reading of Plotinus on God's understanding.

claims.text: Allen argues that Ficino, versed in negative theology, must have been amazed not at the notion that God does not understand as we or the angels do but at its role in the Plotinus passage.

quotes.text: This is demonstrably polemical. Ficino was well grounded in the intricacies of negative theology, the theology that denies the possibility of talking about God except in equivocal terms

Therefore, Ficino, if amazed at all, as Pico claimed, must have been amazed not at the notion that God cannot be said to understand anything in the way we or even the angels understand (for this was an apophatic argument with which he was wholly familiar) but rather at its role in the particular passage in Plotinus.

claims.hedge_words: if amazed at all, as Pico claimed, must have been

bears_on.note: Allen defends Ficino against Pico's charge of misunderstanding.

judged.justification: Reads the Commento's opening barb as unfair to Ficino's negative theology.

claims.text: Allen argues that Pico's account of the three hypostases, identifying the second, which the ancient Neoplatonists called Mind, with Angel or Angelic Mind, is one of his most interesting contributions in the Commento.

quotes.text: One of Pico's most interesting contributions in the Commento is, I would argue, his account of the three hypostases, particularly of the second, which the ancient Neoplatonists had identified with Mind but which he identifies with Angel or Angelic Mind.

judged.justification: Makes the Angelic Mind as second hypostasis the centre of Pico's Neoplatonism in the Commento.

claims.text: Allen says some Neoplatonists put a host of intelligible and intellectual creatures, whom Christians call angels, between the first hypostasis and the World Soul, and that this shows Pico's medievalism since Plotinus spoke simply of Soul.

quotes.text: Some of the Neoplatonists had maintained that between the first hypostasis, God or the One or the Good, and the third hypostasis, the World Soul, came a host of intelligible and intellectual creatures whom Christians call the "angels" - and here Pico reveals his medievalism, since Plotinus had spoken simply of Soul and had argued that the World-Soul is the first instance of this generic Soul.

bears_on.note: Contrast with Plotinus (and the Ficinian Plotinian frame) on the second hypostasis.

claims.text: Allen reports that for the view of an angelic order between the first and third hypostases Pico cites Proclus, Hermias and Syrianus, together with the Areopagite and other Christian theologians, probably alluding to Scotus and Giles of Viterbo.

quotes.text: For this view, Pico specifically cites Proclus, Hermias, and Syrianus (Proclus's teacher), along with the Areopagite and other Christian theologians, probably alluding to Scotus and Giles of Viterbo (since he adduces them later).

judged.justification: Names the Proclean sources Allen finds Pico citing for the angelic second hypostasis.

claims.text: Allen says Pico's terminology certainly draws on Iamblichean and Proclian distinctions between the Ideas and the highest spiritual beings contemplating them, midway between the intelligibles and the intellectual beings below.

quotes.text: In his terminology, he is certainly drawing upon Iamblichian and Proclian distinctions between the Ideas (the pure intelligibles) and the highest spiritual beings contemplating them, who are in turn midway between the intelligibles and the host of intellectual beings below them.

claims.text: Allen reports that the 'more perfect Platonists' whom Pico twice names, among them Plotinus and Porphyry, held that between the first and third hypostases there is only one Mind, called the son of the father, and that Pico prefers this view as closer to Aristotle.

quotes.text: However, those Pico twice calls the "more perfect Platonists," Plotinus and Porphyry among them, had maintained that between the first and third hypostases there is only one Mind, not many minds, and they had even referred to it as the "son" of the father. This view, he says, is also closer to the opinion of Aristotle, and he prefers it because it enables him to explore the ground ... common to both Platonists and Aristotelians

judged.justification: Explains Pico's preference for a single angelic Mind by a concordist motive.

claims.text: Allen says that in the Commento God creates a single Mind from eternity, a perfect effect of a perfect cause and God's sole immediate creation.

quotes.text: From his eternity, God creates this single Mind, and since He is the perfect cause, it is a perfect effect and is unique. This is God's sole creation in the sense that it alone comes "directly" (immediatamente) from him.

claims.text: Allen reports that Pico attacks Ficino for holding, presumably in De amore 4.4, that according to Plato human souls are also created directly by God, a view held by neither Plotinus nor Proclus nor their followers.

quotes.text: And here Pico again attacks Ficino, this time for maintaining (presumably in De amore 4.4) that "according to Plato" human souls are also created directly by God, a view maintained by neither Plotinus nor Proclus nor their followers.

bears_on.note: Pico's attack on Ficino's doctrine that human souls are created directly by God.

claims.text: Allen argues that Pico ignores the Timaeus's Demiurge, who creates human souls directly and the World Soul, and that Pico is either precipitate or radically simplifying.

quotes.text: But Pico is ignoring the problems generated by the Platonic account of the Demiurge in the Timaeus, where the creator God does create human souls directly, while leaving younger gods to fashion the human body; further, this Demiurge cannot be equated with the World Soul, since the Timaeus specifically says that the Demiurge creates the World Soul (30B, 34Bff.). Again either Pico is being precipitate and not acknowledging the complexity of the problems or else he is choosing radically to simplify them.

claims.hedge_words: either Pico is being precipitate and not acknowledging the complexity of the problems or else he is choosing radically to simplify them

open_questions.text: Whether Pico's simplification of the Timaeus's Demiurge is oversight or deliberate is left open.

basis_quote.text: Again either Pico is being precipitate and not acknowledging the complexity of the problems or else he is choosing radically to simplify them.

bears_on.note: Allen finds Pico's polemic against Ficino oversimplifies the Timaeus.

claims.text: Allen says that Pico argues the Platonic Word should not be identified with the Christian Son of God, whereas Ficino does identify them, convinced that Plato foresaw the mystery of the Trinity.

quotes.text: At all events, this first unique creature had been variously called by the ancients "Wisdom" "the Son," "Mind," "Divine Reason," even "The Word," though Pico argues that we should not identify this Platonic Word with the Christian Son of God (yet this is precisely what Ficino does do and is eager to do in the conviction that Plato had foreseen, at least in part, the mystery of the Trinity and the creative if not the redemptive power of the Son).

bears_on.note: Pico refuses the Platonic-Word/Christian-Son identification that Ficino embraces.

judged.justification: Locates a Christological difference between Pico and Ficino in the Commento's angelology.

claims.text: Allen says Pico gives two grounds for not identifying the second hypostasis with the Christian Son: the Son is consubstantial with the Father, and the Son is a creator whereas the second Platonic hypostasis is a creature, identified with the first and noblest angel; God creates Mind as Angel.

quotes.text: Pico's grounds are twofold: there is the familiar theological definition that the Son is of one essence with, is consubstantial with, the Father, and there is the less familiar argument that the Christian Son is a creator whereas the second Platonic hypostasis is a creature and must therefore be identified with the first and noblest angel created by God. God, in short, creates Mind as Angelic Being, as Angel.

judged.justification: States the core of Allen's reading: the Platonic Mind is the first created angel, not the Son.

claims.text: Allen says that for the Neoplatonists the first emanation from the One is the emergence of thought, and that God has created the Ideas in the first Mind, giving the intelligible world of which the sensible world is an image.

quotes.text: For the Neoplatonists, if not Plato himself, the first progression or emanation from the One (it is not a "creation" per se) is not the creation of the world but the emergence of thought and of thinking, defined as intelligible being. But since God has created the Ideas or Forms of all things in that first Mind, where they have their formal being, he has created in it the intelligible world, and our sensible world, governed in its entirety by the World Soul, is an image and likeness of this Idea world.

claims.text: Allen reports Pico saying the ancient theologians equated God with Uranus, Mind with Cronus (Saturn), and the World Soul with Jupiter, Uranus standing for preeminence, Saturn for intellectuality, Jupiter for active rule over inferiors.

quotes.text: The ancient theologians, he says, had "concealed their mysteries under poetic veils," meaning in effect under the veils of mythology. They had equated God with Uranus, Mind with Cronus (Saturn), and the World Soul with Jupiter, observing the following basic principle: Uranus must stand for anything that is preeminent (as the firmament is preeminent), Saturn for "the property of being intellectual," and Jupiter for "the ... property of being active" in ruling over inferiors.

judged.justification: Gives the mythological key to the Commento's three hypostases.

claims.text: Allen says the triple principle of Uranus, Cronus and Zeus derives from etymologies in Plato's Cratylus, and that Ficino sets out the same arguments in his Phaedrus commentary.

quotes.text: This triple principle is derived in fact from the etymologies explored in Plato's Cratylus, where Uranus is the upward-regarding or contemplative power, Cronus the self-regarding or self-reflective power, and Zeus the downward-regarding or regulative power. Ficino sets out the same set of arguments in his Phaedrus commentary.

bears_on.note: Pico and Ficino share the Cratylus-derived triad.

claims.text: Allen says both Florentines accept Proclian-inspired equations letting Saturn exercise a Uranian or Jovian power, but Pico breaks with Ficino in denying that Uranus can exercise a Saturnian power because he transcends the intellect entirely.

quotes.text: Both Florentine thinkers understood the Proclian-inspired equations that allow for Saturn to exercise at times a Uranian or a Jovian power or for Uranus to exercise a Jovian power, though Pico breaks with Ficino in denying that Uranus can exercise a Saturnian power on the grounds that he transcends the intellect entirely.

bears_on.note: Pico breaks with Ficino over whether Uranus can exercise a Saturnian power; his ground is Uranus's transcendence of intellect.

judged.justification: Pinpoints a specific doctrinal point of divergence from Ficino on the first hypostasis's relation to intellect.

claims.text: Allen says these equations presuppose that any deity can exercise all these powers, since each deity is in its way all the others, a monotheistic system concealed beneath a polytheistic rind, so that readings of a deity or its daemons must be careful and may run in parallel.

quotes.text: For these equations presuppose that any deity can exercise any or all of these powers on the grounds that each deity is in its own way all other deities in what is in essence a monotheistic system concealed beneath a polytheistic rind. It also means that any reference to a deity, or indeed to the deity's attendant daemons, has to be interpreted with extreme care, since several readings are simultaneously possible and at times may even run in parallel.

claims.text: Allen says Pico identifies the Platonic Mind as the first and noblest angel and as the intelligible world within it, the Ideas of all things later created, a creature as perfect as a created thing can be.

quotes.text: Pico is led to confront some of the key problems associated with the Platonic Mind, which he identifies as the first and "noblest" angel and as the intelligible world within it, that is, as the Ideas or Forms of all things that will be created subsequent to it. Since it has been created, and created solely by God, it is a creature "as perfect as it is possible for a created thing to be."

claims.text: Allen says Pico, thinking in an Aristotelian way, treats Angel or Mind as compounded of potency and act, equating potency with the unlimited of the Philebus and a kind of matter, and act with the limit and form.

quotes.text: and yet it consists for Pico, who is thinking here in an Aristotelian way, of potency and act, the former being inferior to the latter. Potency he hastens to equate with "the unlimited" in the famous passage in the Philebus (23 Cff.), and act he equates with "the limit," and then suggests that in some sense at least the former is a kind of matter (though matter differs with differing levels of being) and that the latter is form.
In regard to this being, Angel or Mind is compounded of two contrary principles, like every other created thing existing between the two uncompounded extremes of God and prime matter.

judged.justification: Angel as composite of potency and act, an Aristotelian gloss on the Platonic second hypostasis.

claims.text: Allen says Mind, identified with Saturn, has three functions: contemplation of higher things (which Ficino was to call Uranian), self-contemplation (which Ficino was to call self-regarding), and a Jovian downward providential regard of the universe it creates.

quotes.text: But Mind, identified hypostatically with Saturn, nonetheless has three functions - a Saturnian contemplation of (Ficino was to call this, more logically, a Uranian regarding of) things higher than itself (but such can only be God); a Saturnian contemplation "that stays within itself" (Ficino was to call this self-regarding), that is, a contemplation of itself as the first, most perfect creature; and a Jovian downward, providential regarding of the universe it ... creates.

bears_on.note: Allen notes Ficino's later relabelling of Pico's Saturnian functions as Uranian and self-regarding.

claims.text: Allen argues that Pico's attribution of Mind's upward regard to act, self-regard to act and potency and downward regard to potency is a sleight of hand that becomes untenable given his own identification of potency with matter and act with form.

quotes.text: Pico performs a sleight of hand here by attributing Mind's Saturnian (Uranian) regard upward to its act, its Saturnian regard self-ward to its act and potency, and its Jovian regard downward to its potency. But this distribution becomes untenable if we introduce his identifications of potency with matter and act with form. For Mind's Jovian regard downward is an extending downward not of its matter but of its form, an exercising not of its limitlessness but of its limit.

open_questions.text: Allen holds the Commento's distribution of potency and act across Mind's three functions incoherent; the source reading may differ.

basis_quote.text: But this distribution becomes untenable if we introduce his identifications of potency with matter and act with form.

claims.text: Allen says Mind, as first one-and-many and first angel and the plenitude of the Ideas, is the first unitary composite and first beautiful thing, the composite universal beauty that Ficino would call the splendor of the Ideas.

quotes.text: Moreover, since Mind is the first one-and-many and exists both as the first angel and as the plenitude of the Ideas, it is the first unitary composite and therefore the first beautiful thing: not so much the absolute, exemplary unique Idea of Beauty as the composite, manifold, universal beauty, the splendor, Ficino would consistently call it, of all the Ideas

bears_on.note: Allen says Ficino would consistently call this composite beauty the splendor of the Ideas.

claims.text: Allen reports Pico's definition in Commento 2.8 of such beauty as a friendly enmity or harmonious discord, backed by Heraclitus and Empedocles, and that only God is without contrariety while Angel and Beauty are composed of potency and act.

quotes.text: But such beauty, he argues in 2.8, is the result of both discord and concord, of unity and of contrariety, of Venus's companionship with Mars: "This can be taken as a true definition of such beauty: it is nothing other than a friendly enmity, or a harmonious discord." In addition, he cites Heraclitus on strife as the father of all things and Empedocles on the ever-during alternation of love and strife.
Only God is without contrariety or discord, whereas Angel and Beauty alike are composed of potency and act, of discord and concord.

claims.text: Allen believes the lemmata about Love's birth on the birth day of Venus, when Porus had joined Penia in the gardens of Jupiter, are the greatest mystery of the Symposium for Pico and occasioned some of his most fertile ideas as a Platonizing hermeneut.

quotes.text: For a Platonic elucidation of this fundamental metaphysical issue, Pico turns to an amalgam of the lemmata in the memorable account of Love's birth attributed by Socrates to Diotima in the Symposium (203Bff.): "Love was born in the gardens of Jupiter on the birth day of Venus, after Porus had joined with Penia, all the gods being seated at the banquet, and Porus himself, the son of counsel, being drunk with nectar." For it is these lemmata that constitute, I believe, the greatest mystery of the Symposium for Pico and that occasioned some of his most fertile ideas as a Platonizing hermeneut.

judged.justification: Centres the Poros/Penia lemmata as the seat of Pico's angelic-Mind doctrine.

claims.text: Allen reports that in Commento 2.13 Pico asserts an unformed substance trailed after God, originally prime matter, which when given form by God became Angel-Mind.

quotes.text: In 2.13, he asserts that after God Himself, there trailed "an unformed substance" (quella natura informe) that must originally have been prime matter; but when it was given form by God, it became Angel-Mind, the form consisting of the Ideas that emerge from God as their source and that collectively constitute Beauty.

claims.text: Allen says that the Ideas have causal being in God, formal being in Mind, which is counselled by God, and participated being in rational Soul, and that Pico's arguments about the unformed substance look at first self-contradictory.

quotes.text: This is at first glance a series of self-contradictory arguments, particularly so in light of the proposition at the end of book 1, namely, that the Ideas have (1) their causal being in God and are therefore not in God; (2) their formal being in Mind, who "is counseled" by God (meaning furnished with the ... Ideas needed to make this sensible world); and (3) their participated being in (rational) Soul, where they are called rational principles or reasons.

claims.text: Allen says the Commento exposes a real and enduring problem in the Neoplatonic emanatory system: Mind without the Ideas must have been unformed, in potency, and quasi-matter.

quotes.text: But it underscores a real and enduring problem in the Neoplatonic emanatory system: Mind without the Ideas must have been not only unformed but also, in a way, in potency, unlimited, in a state (however we may define such a state) of imperfection, of what Pico here calls an "opacity." Consequently, it must have been a quasi-matter.

open_questions.text: How the Neoplatonic emanatory system can describe Mind before it holds the Ideas.

basis_quote.text: But it underscores a real and enduring problem in the Neoplatonic emanatory system

claims.text: Allen reports that in Pico's account angelic Mind, once it holds the Ideas' imperfectly seen beauty, comes to desire them in perfect form; Allen adds that this desire is the first instance of love though Pico never says so.

quotes.text: Pico goes on to demarcate yet further intermediate stages: with the coming of the Ideas, Mind does indeed contain their beauty within itself, but problematically, since "that beauty is still imperfect and obscured by the darkness, the opacity of Mind's own substance." Hence, "there inevitably arises in angelic Mind a desire to possess the Ideas in their perfect form," and this desire is a desire for beauty and constitutes therefore (though Pico never exactly says this) the first instance of love.

claims.text: Allen says that in the reading he gives Pico, Love is born when Porus, the multitude of the Ideas in Mind, unites with Penia, the unformed deficient Jovian state of that essence, an act-potency union that gives rise to Mind as Paradise.

quotes.text: Thus Love is born when Porus (Plenty), meaning the multitude of the Ideas in Mind, is united with Penia (Need), meaning, not the essence per se of Mind, but the unformed, deficient, or imperfect state, the Jovian state, of that essence, which Pico sees Plato signifying in the Symposium's image of "the gardens of Jupiter" (203B). This birth moment is the uniting of act with potency, the planting of the Ideas in the garden of Mind, a planting that gives rise to Paradise, or rather to Mind as Paradise.

judged.justification: Reads Poros/Penia as act and potency within the angelic Mind, not a myth of soul.

claims.text: Allen says Pico stumbles in declaring that desire was born from the union of the perfect state of the Ideas, signified by Porus, son of Counsel that is of God, and their imperfect state, signified by Penia; and reports the birthday of Venus as the day when the beauty of the Ideas first descended into Angelic Mind.

quotes.text: Pico stumbles, however, when he goes on to declare that the desire was born from a union between the perfect state of the Ideas, signified by Porus, the son of Counsel, that is, of God, and the Ideas' defective or imperfect state in the incomplete, unformed substance, signified by Penia. Love could only be born after ideal Beauty had been born in Mind; thus it was born on Venus's birthday, later defined as the day "when the beauty of the Ideas first descended into Angelic Mind."

claims.text: Allen says Pico lost interest in the Commento project but did extract some formulations from it in preparing the Heptaplus.

quotes.text: in the whole project, as his "council" and other issues became more pressing, though he did extract some formulations from the Commento in preparing his Heptaplus.

judged.justification: Allen's own statement of a Commento-to-Heptaplus link, thin as it is.

claims.text: Allen reports that in Pico's account Love, once born, turns Mind to God, which receives from him the perfecting of the beauty of the Ideas, and only then does Venus become a fully grown goddess.

quotes.text: Nonetheless, Love was born at that time in Mind, born as the desire "to possess more perfectly that beauty it already possessed in some measure [gia in qualche modo avea]" but not fully. Awakened by this love, Mind turned toward God "and received from Him the perfecting of the beauty of the Ideas." And only then when Mind possessed the Ideas and their beauty did Venus become a fully grown goddess, "that is, reached perfection in Mind."

claims.text: Allen reports that Pico takes the gods seated at the banquet, in the Pythagorean-Parmenidean manner, to mean the Ideas, which precede Venus since she is the beauty that results from all the Ideas.

quotes.text: On this natal day, however, the gods were seated at the banquet, the gods meaning, in the Pythagorean-Parmenidean manner, says Pico, the Ideas which precede Venus herself, ... since she is the beauty or grace, he reiterates, which results from all the Ideas.

claims.text: Allen says Pico takes Porus drunk with nectar to signify the sheer multiplicity of the Ideas, and that Pico concludes 2.13 by saying the Ideas of other things existed in the Angelic Mind but were not welcomed to the banquet since immortality was not granted them.

quotes.text: Pico takes Plato's description of Porus as drunk with nectar to signify "the sheer multiplicity of the Ideas" (l'affluenzia universale d'esse idee), presumably the Ideas of all the other things that were there in Mind, or possibly all the Ideas not yet signified by the gods who were invited to the banquet and who formally and causally preceded Venus.

For, he concludes 2.13 with the argument that "although the Ideas of other things existed in the Angelic Mind, Plato does not say that they were welcomed to the banquet, because the gift of immortality was not granted to them."

claims.text: Allen reports that Pico resolves the paradox of Love as oldest and youngest god by holding that Love existed before the other gods, the Ideas, who achieved perfected being only after Love caused Mind to return to the One, yet is the youngest because the other gods existed before him joined to the unformed substance of Mind.

quotes.text: Pico resolves the apparent paradox by declaring that Love is the oldest god, because he existed before the other gods, who, as the Ideas, were to achieve their "natural" or "perfected" being only after Love had caused Mind to return to the One and in turn to receive its natural being; in other words, the Ideas were still in Mind imperfectly (secondo il loro essere ideale imperfetto). But he is the youngest and the most beautiful god, because the other gods existed before him, not, as one might have anticipated from Pico's earlier arguments, in their cause, the One, but rather joined to the still unformed substance of Mind in an ideal but imperfect way.

claims.text: Allen says Love is a mysterious paidogeron, a child-father, whose birth in the unformed substance of angelic Mind from the mixing of Porus and Penia coincides with the birth of his still infant mother Venus, though Pico does not pursue the paradox.

quotes.text: An old-young god, therefore, though Pico does not pursue the paradox, he is a mysterious paidogeron, a child-father, who has not even been conceived on the day that Venus was born and the gods banqueted together in celebration of her coming. And yet on that very day in the gardens of Jupiter - that is, in "the unformed substance of angelic Mind" and from the mixing of the perfection of the Ideas, which is Porus, with their imperfection and their want of being perfect, which is Penia, "poor and indigent, being devoid of all being and all act" (d'ogni essere e d'ogni atto priva) - Love was born, even as his mother was still a babe.

claims.text: Allen says Ficino had confronted the same conundrums in De amore 5.10 and 1.3, and that both thinkers are struck by the Orphic bosom of chaos and argue that Mind was in a sense a chaos waiting to be a cosmos.

quotes.text: Interestingly, Ficino had confronted the same conundrums in his De amore, both at 5.10 and earlier at 1.3, when he attempted his own unfolding of the mystery of Mind and its threefold emanation from, turning back toward, and returning to the One. Both thinkers are struck by the Orphic notion of the "bosom of chaos" and argue that Mind was in a sense a chaos, a chaos waiting nonetheless to be a cosmos.

bears_on.note: Allen finds Pico and Ficino treating the same Orphic chaos and Mind conundrum.

judged.justification: Shows convergence, not only quarrel, between Pico and Ficino on angelic Mind.

claims.text: Allen reports that Pico, citing Orphic verses in 2.14 and 2.22, says Mind could rightly be called a chaos when first filled with all the Ideas, still imperfect, indistinct and confused.

quotes.text: Pico adduces the Orphic verses in 2.14 and 2.22 and observes that Mind could "rightly be called a chaos" when it was first filled with all the Ideas and the Ideas were still "imperfect, indistinct as it were, and confused."

claims.text: Allen says that in Pico's account Mind, to perfect the Ideas, must revert to God and unite with him, completing what Pico calls the first circle, and then possesses the beauty of the Ideas in perfection so that Venus becomes a sovereign goddess in Mind.

quotes.text: Since the Ideas can be perfected only when they are separated from what is alien to them, separated in effect from the as yet unformed chaos of Mind and returned to their source in the One, Mind must itself revert to God and unite with him. Thus Mind completes what Pico calls "the first circle" (il primo circuit) of returning to its own first and final cause and to the Ideas' first cause, namely, to the unity of God. When it does so, it possesses the beauty of the Ideas in their perfection, and at that point Venus becomes adult, becomes a perfect, a sovereign goddess in Mind.

judged.justification: The return of angelic Mind to God as a complete circle: the metaphysical frame for the Death of the Kiss.

claims.text: Allen says that despite this circle Mind eventually succumbs to time in what seems the onset of a Saturnian aging, being overthrown by its youngest son Jupiter, the World Soul, who escapes being swallowed by being replaced with a stone.

quotes.text: Despite this ideal triadic encircling of Mind and the notion of its return and perfection, eventually Mind succumbs to time in what seems to be the onset of a Saturnian aging and fatigue, succumbs, that is, to a new inferior order. In the Ancients' poetic mythology, Jupiter, the World Soul, escapes being consumed by Saturn, as thoughts are consumed by their thinker: in his stead, his father is given a stone (the stone of the sensible world, of sensible images and data) to swallow down.

claims.text: Allen says that for both Pico and Ficino the succession myth expresses the violence of hypostatic succession and Soul's emergence from Mind, but that it no longer seems to accommodate Pico's initial account of Love and Beauty.

quotes.text: For Pico and Ficino, this violent revolution or succession myth, like other such myths, speaks to a fundamental aspect of the Neoplatonic metaphysics of emanation: the mystery of the violence involved in the hypostatic succession, the wrenching descent of levels of being, and in Jupiter's particular case the violence integral to Soul's emergence from Mind. But it no longer seems to accommodate Pico's initial account of Love and Beauty.

bears_on.note: Allen treats the succession-myth reading as shared by Pico and Ficino.

claims.text: Allen says Pico turned to another Venus of the Symposium, the heavenly Venus, daughter of Uranus, who was born a perfect nymph from the sea's foam when Uranus's sperm cast by Saturn fell into the waves of matter.

quotes.text: Accordingly, he turned to the unfolding of another of the Symposium's mysteries: Plato's reference at 180D-E to another Venus, the daughter of Uranus. This, the heavenly Venus, had another birthday altogether, since she was never a babe but was born a perfect nymph, a Nereid from the sea's foam, when Uranus's sperm was cast by Saturn as he cut off his father's testicles into the waves of matter.

claims.text: Allen says Pico knew that Proclus and other antique interpreters taught that all traditional myths were theological at heart, and that Dionysius the Areopagite had stressed in On the Celestial Hierarchy that the more repellent the myth the more profound its hidden mystery.

quotes.text: particularly when we recall that he was well aware that Proclus and other antique interpreters had taught, following the lead of the mythological passages in Plato's dialogues, that all the traditional myths were theological at heart and that one had to exercise extreme subtlety and inventiveness rather than caution in their exposition. Indeed, the more repellent the myth, the more profound its hidden mystery and the greater the distinction-making skill and zeal expected of its interpreter, as Dionysius the Areopagite had stressed in his work On the Celestial Hierarchy (2.3).

judged.justification: Links Pico's Commento exegetical method to Proclus and the Areopagite on repellent myths.

claims.text: Allen says the myth of the Anadyomene spurred Pico to suggest that the sea was the unformed substance first found in Mind, the primal Oceanus or Neptune as certain Platonists maintained, and that Venus was in this sense united with Mind.

quotes.text: The myth of the Anadyomene certainly spurred Pico into boldly suggesting that the sea was the unformed substance that was first found in Mind and was the primal Oceanus or Neptune, as certain Platonists had maintained, and that in sense Venus was united with Mind. He turns for confirmation to references in Moses, David, Origen, and Pletho to the effect that "waters" are a recurring image for the seas "upon which God founded the whole world."

claims.text: Allen says that since Uranus as God creates only the first angel, whom the Platonists call Mind and the poets Saturn, God is figuratively sterile once he has created Mind, having been in a way castrated by Mind.

quotes.text: Since Uranus, as God, creates only the first angel, "whom the Platonists call Mind, and the poets, Saturn," who in turn creates the rest of the universe, God is figuratively sterile after he has created Mind, having been in a way castrated by Mind.

judged.justification: Allen's compact statement of the Uranus-Saturn identification with God and the first angel.

claims.text: Allen says Pico avoids reconciling Saturn as castrator with Saturn as himself the foam-flecked sea, the unformed substance of Mind impregnated by Uranus's sperm, which Pico allegorizes as the plenitude of the Ideas.

quotes.text: But Pico avoids reconciling the notion of Saturn as castrator with the notion of Saturn as himself the foam-flecked sea, the unformed matter or substance of Mind, which is impregnated by the sperm from Uranus's testicles, allegorized by Pico as "the plenitude of the Ideas."

open_questions.text: How Saturn as castrator and Saturn as the sea of unformed substance are to be reconciled is left unresolved by Pico, on Allen's reading.

basis_quote.text: But Pico avoids reconciling the notion of Saturn as castrator with the notion of Saturn as himself the foam-flecked sea

claims.text: Allen says Pico identifies the unformed substance of Mind with the Necessity of the Timaeus, so that the Ideas first came into Mind in the reign of Necessity, only becoming perfected in the reign of Love when Mind turned to God.

quotes.text: Moreover, since he also identifies this substance with the Necessity of the Timaeus (47Eff.), he can argue that the Ideas first came into Mind during the reign of Necessity and were thus not yet in their perfect state; only in the succeeding reign of Love, when Mind turned to God, did the imperfect Ideas within it become perfected.

claims.text: Allen says Pico in these arguments treads a tightrope between inherited mythological contradictions and Neoplatonic attempts to distinguish stages in the emanation of being.

quotes.text: In all these arguments, based as they are on the gift of the Ideas to a still imperfect Mind and on the identification of Venus with the collective splendor and yet variety of the Ideas, Pico treads a tightrope across the chasm, on the one hand, of inherited mythological contradictions and, on the other, of various Neoplatonic attempts to distinguish the stages in the emanation, not only of becoming, but of being itself

claims.text: Allen thinks that behind the Neoplatonic allegoresis of the Commento there looms for Pico, much more than for Ficino, the authority and ever presence of Genesis.

quotes.text: Behind all this Neoplatonic allegoresis, with its unveiling of myth-inspired notions of the emanation and procession of the Ideas, of Mind, of the two Venuses, and of their accompanying Loves, there looms for Pico - and for Pico much more, I think, than for Ficino - the authority and the ever presence of Genesis.

bears_on.note: Allen's contrast: Genesis looms larger for Pico than for Ficino.

judged.justification: Ties the Commento's Neoplatonic myth-reading to the biblical foundation of the Heptaplus.

claims.text: Allen reports that in the proem to the second exposition of the Heptaplus Pico declares Genesis to excel all other progeny of the human mind in doctrine, eloquence and genius, though Moses speaks with a veiled face.

quotes.text: the authority and the ever presence of Genesis. This is not only the definitive account for the Judeo-Christian tradition of the beginning of things, it excels, Pico declares in the proem to the second exposition of the Heptaplus, "all other progeny of the human mind in doctrine, eloquence, and genius," even as it is the product of Moses ... having to speak "with a veiled face" (velata facie).

claims.text: Allen says the Heptaplus of 1489 gives a sevenfold interpretation of the six days of creation and the seventh day of rest, with an appendix on the Bible's opening phrase, approaching Genesis by way of Christology and Neoplatonic metaphysics.

quotes.text: For a consideration of what Genesis, or more particularly its first twenty-seven verses, meant to a Neoplatonizing Pico, we must turn to this Heptaplus of 1489, where he produced a sevenfold interpretation of the six days of the Biblical creation and of the seventh day of God's rest and added in an appendix a Cabalistic reading of the Bible's opening phrase. In this complex treatise, the Mosaic account of creation is approached by way of two dominant perspectives: the perspective, predictably for a Christian, of Christology and the perspective, once again, of Neoplatonic metaphysics and allegorizing

judged.justification: Allen's frame for the Heptaplus: Christology plus Neoplatonic metaphysics.

claims.text: Allen argues that for Pico, unlike for Ficino with the Timaeus, Moses's first book took precedence and became the most profound of Platonic texts, letting him look beyond the Platonic dialogues as the Parmenides let Proclus and his successors.

quotes.text: But whatever the allure for Ficino of Plato's Timaeus, for Pico Moses's first book took precedence, and eventually it dominated his attempt to understand the origin of things Platonically. Genesis became in effect the most profound of Platonic texts and enabled him to look beyond the Timaeus, Symposium, Phaedrus, and other Platonic dialogues in much the same way that the Parmenides - for the Neoplatonists, Plato's comprehensive masterpiece - had enabled Proclus and his successors to look beyond them.

bears_on.note: Allen contrasts Ficino's Timaeus-centred creation account with Pico's Genesis-centred one.

judged.justification: Reads the Heptaplus as Pico's Genesis-based analogue of the Proclean move beyond the dialogues.

claims.text: Allen reports that in the Heptaplus proem to Lorenzo de' Medici Pico says Moses philosophizes on the emanation of all things from God and on the grade, number and order of the parts of the world, beneath the rough bark of its words.

quotes.text: In a proem to the Heptaplus which is addressed to Lorenzo de' Medici, Pico observes that Moses "most loftily philosophizes on the emanation of all things from God, and on the grade, number, and order of the parts of the world," and that beneath "the rough bark [rudi cortice] of its words," Genesis, and preeminently its opening, has divine depths requiring interpretation by those who have achieved maturity of judgment

claims.text: Allen reports that Pico asserts Genesis requires a self-consistent and coherent course of interpretation, interpreting the whole creation continuously and without confusion in seven senses, and asserts nothing alien to nature or to the truths ascertained by the better philosophers.

quotes.text: He is anxious to assert, furthermore, not merely that Moses is a deep philosopher, but more particularly, first, that Genesis requires "a self-consistent and coherent course of interpretation," despite its apparent "perplexity, ambiguity and variety," for it is planned in such a way that it interprets "the entire creation of the world continuously and without confusion in not merely one but seven senses," and, second, that it does not assert "anything strange or wonderful or alien to the nature of things as they are observed, or to the truths ascertained by the better philosophers."

claims.text: Allen reports that in the proem to the second exposition Pico defines Moses's aim as arranging discourse so that the same words, context and order are suitable for symbolizing the secrets of all the worlds and of the whole of nature.

quotes.text: In the proem to the second exposition, Pico defines Moses's aim, "truly carried out with divine rather than human diligence," as follows: "to use terms and to arrange his discourse so that the same words, the same context, and the same order in the whole passage are completely suitable for symbolizing the secrets of all the worlds and of the ... whole of nature."

claims.text: Allen reports that in the second general proem Pico outlines the ancient philosophers' doctrine of the three worlds: the supercelestial world, which the theologians call the angelic and the philosophers the intelligible world, the celestial, and the sublunary.

quotes.text: In the second general proem, Pico proceeds to outline the ancient philosophers' doctrine of the three worlds which he also finds in Genesis: the ultramundane or supercelestial world, "which the theologians call the angelic and the philosophers call the intelligible world" of light and which is symbolized by fire; the celestial world of the stars and planets, of darkness and light together, which is symbolized by fire and water; and the sublunary world of darkness we inhabit, which is symbolized by water.

judged.justification: Identifies the supercelestial world of the Heptaplus with the angelic and the Neoplatonic intelligible world.

claims.text: Allen reports Pico assigning eternal life and unchanging activity to the first world, stable life with changing activity to the second, and alternation of life and death to the third, the third moved by the second and the second governed by the first.

quotes.text: Pico proceeds to assign eternal life and unchanging activity to the first, partaking as it does of the divine nature of mind; stability of life but change of activity and position to the second, partaking as it does of incorruptible body and of mind enslaved to that body; and perpetual alternation of life and death to the third, composed as it is of corruptible body. The third is moved by the second, while the second, whose outermost sphere is the prime mover, is governed by the first.

claims.text: Allen reports Pico saying that the three worlds are one world since whatever is in all the worlds together is also contained in each separately.

quotes.text: But "these three worlds are one world" in that "whatever is in all the worlds together is also contained in each of the worlds separately."

claims.text: Allen says Pico is surely invoking two Neoplatonic formulas, that the whole is in the part according to the part's capacity and that all things are in all things, each in its own way, which Proclus had refined as keys to the unity of the world.

quotes.text: Here, surely, Pico is invoking the two celebrated Neoplatonic formulas to the effect that the whole is in the part, though according to the capacity of the part, and that all things are in all things, though each in its own way or in a certain way. These formulas had been refined by Proclus in the belief that they were the key to our understanding of the unity of the world, of the oneness that makes the intelligible world a many and a one.

judged.justification: Names a Proclean formula behind the mutual containment of the three worlds.

claims.text: Allen reports that Pico says whatever is in the lower world is in the higher ones in better form, and that the supercelestial world has the Idea of heat, apparently the love of the seraphic intellects, and the understanding of the cherubic intellects corresponds to water.

quotes.text: For Pico continues, "Whatever is in the lower world is also in the higher ones, but of better stamp," and contrariwise "whatever is in the higher ones is also seen in the lowest but in a degenerate condition." Thus our elemental world has the heat and fire which burns, while the celestial world has the heating power of the sun, which gives us life, and the supercelestial world has the Idea of heat, identified apparently with the love of the seraphic intellects. Similarly, what is water here is the Moon in the heavens and the understanding of the cherubic intellects in the supercelestial realm.

claims.text: Allen reports that Pico correlates the nine orders of angels, presided over by God's unmoving unity, with the nine heavenly spheres presided over by the unmoving empyrean, and these with nine spheres of corruptible forms founded on prime matter.

quotes.text: The nine orders of the angels presided over by God's unmoving unity correspond to the nine revolving heavenly spheres presided over by the unmoving empyrean, and these correspond in turn to the nine spheres of ever-moving corruptible forms founded upon prime matter.

judged.justification: Nine angelic orders as the top of a nine-nine-nine correspondence in the Heptaplus.

claims.text: Allen reports Pico saying the worlds, bound by the chains of concord, exchange natures and names with mutual liberality, so that Nature is an allegory full of hidden alliances and affinities.

quotes.text: Moreover, "bound by the chains of concord," writes Pico, "all these worlds exchange natures as well as names with mutual liberality." Thus Nature herself is an allegory full of "hidden alliances and affinities" that enable an enlightened interpreter to work by way of the correspondences between the worlds.

claims.text: Allen says an Empedoclean vision of nature riven by discord seems foreign to Pico, perhaps because it is too dualistic, the intelligible realm being governed by the concord of Castor and Pollux.

quotes.text: By implication at least, Nature must also be riven by discord: countering every hidden alliance and affinity must be ruptures and oppositions. To every attraction of like to like - to invoke the ancient saw - there must be the corresponding repulsion of unlike from unlike. But such an Empedoclean vision seems to be foreign to Pico, perhaps because it is too dualisdc. However divided our fallen world may be by the discord caused by a Helen or a Clytemnestra, the intelligible realm is governed by the concord of a Castor and Pollux

claims.hedge_words: seems to be foreign to Pico, perhaps because it is too dualisdc

open_questions.text: Allen does not reconcile this with the Commento's definition of beauty as friendly enmity and his citing of Empedocles on love and strife.

basis_quote.text: But such an Empedoclean vision seems to be foreign to Pico, perhaps because it is too dualisdc.

claims.text: Allen says Pico wants to postulate a separate fourth world for man, in whom are found all the things of the sublunar, celestial and supercelestial worlds.

quotes.text: Furthermore, we might have expected in the final, the sensitive, triad a division into zoophytes, beasts, and man rather than into zoophytes, lower animals, and higher animals. But Pico wants to postulate a separate, a fourth, world for man, in whom are found all those things in the three other worlds, the sublunar, the celestial, and the supercelestial.

judged.justification: Man as fourth world alongside the three worlds in Allen's reading.

claims.text: Allen says that because Moses's scripture is the exact image of the world each word must be interpreted in terms of the four worlds, with a fifth exposition on discordant concord, a sixth on fifteen ways things are joined, and a sabbatical exposition on the return of creatures to God.

quotes.text: Since the scripture of Moses is the "exact image of the world" and is arranged, as Exodus 25:40 had declared, "according to the pattern that God had shown him on the mountain," its every word can and must be interpreted in terms of the four worlds. Even so, a fifth land of exposition is needed to explain how the natures are distinct and at the same time united "by a certain discordant concord" and knotted and linked together "by many kinds of interwoven chains," and a sixth kind is needed to explain the fifteen ways we can understand "how one thing is joined or related to another."
Finally, Pico's interpretation comes to rest in a sabbatical exposition of "the felicity of all creatures and their return to God."

judged.justification: Allen's architecture: four world-based expositions, discordant concord, fifteen ways, sabbath.

claims.text: Allen says that because Moses treats all worlds in the same words, each reading must pertain both to sublunar nature and translunar heavens and be consonant with a theological account of the angelic realm and the realm of Mind.

quotes.text: Since "whatever is in any of the worlds is contained in each," Moses, as an "imitator [aemulator] of nature" and in effect as an adept in allegoresis and correspondence theory, necessarily "had to treat of each of these worlds in such a way that in the same words and in the same context he could treat equally of all." Transposed into a Platonic key, this means that each reading must pertain to, and hence explain, both sublunar nature and the translunar heavens and be at the same time fully consonant with a theological account of the angelic realm and the realm of Mind.

judged.justification: Equates the angelic realm of the Heptaplus with the realm of Mind under a Platonic transposition.

claims.text: Allen says the method of the Heptaplus implies that natural science, theology and anthropology share one methodology and hermeneutics, a reading in one being keyed by isomorphic analogies to a parallel reading in another.

quotes.text: Moreover, a proper understanding of man, an enlightened anthropology, will be consonant with such a concomitant natural science ... and theology, and the three disciplines will share the same fundamental methodology and hermeneutics. A reading in one discipline will not only set up resonances in another but be keyed, by way of the isomorphic structure of the analogies established by God at the creation, to a particular parallel reading in that other discipline.

claims.text: Allen says that, like other medieval and ancient texts and like Pico's own Commento, the Heptaplus's central engagement is with another authoritative text, here the opening verses of the Bible.

quotes.text: Pico's Heptaplus may first strike one, for all its boldness, as an essentially medieval work in which the theological concerns take precedence over a concern with the recalcitrant variety of the physical world, though this is very much the theme of the first exposition. Furthermore, like other medieval and indeed ancient texts, and like Pico's own Commento, as we have seen, its central engagement is with another authoritative text, in this case the Bible's opening verses.

judged.justification: Allen's statement of the structural kinship of Heptaplus and Commento: both are exegetical engagements with an authoritative text.

claims.text: Allen says the Heptaplus is original in turning to the Cabala and in making Genesis a Christological, anthropocentric text, the seventh chapter of each of the seven expositions turning to the Son of Man as the definitive law and first and final cause.

quotes.text: The Heptaplus is also original, however, in its turning aside to the Cabala and in its fashioning out of Genesis a Christological text (and by implication an anthropological or anthropocentric one) and thus articulating a human-dominated worldview, for the seventh chapter of each of the seven expositions turns to the Son of Man as the definitive "law," the key to all physics, to all metaphysics, to all theologies, the first and the final cause.

judged.justification: Christological closure of each Heptaplus exposition.

claims.text: Allen says the Heptaplus is a summa of a cosmology of harmony, correspondence and consonance, drawing on Plato's Pythagorean themes and the Neoplatonists, including Dionysius the Areopagite, whom Pico still took to be the Athenian disciple of St. Paul.

quotes.text: It is also remarkable as a summa presenting on the eve of the scientific revolution a cosmology governed by the principles of harmony, correspondence, and consonance. In doing so, it may be harking back to Boethius and Aristotle, but more obviously it is still drawing on Plato's Pythagorean themes and on their elaboration by the Neoplatonists, including Dionysius the Areopagite, whom Pico, like most Renaissance scholars, still assumed was the Athenian disciple of St. Paul mentioned in Acts 17:34.

judged.justification: Places Dionysius among the Neoplatonic sources of the Heptaplus, on the pre-Valla authorship assumption.

claims.text: Allen says that in the Oration other creatures, including the planetary souls and the angelic intellects above them, have natures confining them to a realm of being, whereas the first man can sculpt himself into a beast or a seraph.

quotes.text: Whereas other creatures, including the celestial planetary souls and the ... angelic intellects above them, have "natures" which confine them to a particular realm of being, the first made man is not so confined. As the "molder and maker of himself," he can sculpt himself into whatsoever form he pleases, be it that of a beast or a seraph.

claims.text: Allen reports that in Commento 1.12 Pico defines human nature as the tie and knot of the world and correlates man's parts with the world: body with the material realm, vegetative part with plants, sensitive part with animals, intellectual part with the angels, unity with God.

quotes.text: In 1.12 of the latter, Pico had already defined "human nature" as "the tie and knot of the world," being located in the middle of the ontological hierarchy, and had asserted that man "through his various parts has some relation or correspondence to every part of the world," first his body corresponding to the material realm; his second, vegetative part to the plant realm; his third, sensitive part to the irrational animals; his fifth, intellectual part to the angels; and his sixth part, his unity, to God himself.

judged.justification: Angels as the correspondent of man's intellectual part, in the Commento, before the Heptaplus.

claims.text: Allen says Pico seems to suggest in Commento 2.6 that the world is the great man, the macroanthropos, and that this is for Pico a Mosaic trope as his gematria-based epilogue on Bereshit shows.

quotes.text: At all events, the notion of man as the little world and by predication of the world (or World Soul, as Pico seems to suggest in 2.6) as the great man, the macroanthropos, has rather different implications for our understanding of man's relationship both to nature in general and to his own human nature than does the image of Proteus. And this despite the fact that the world as a great man is also an ancient trope and for Pico at least a Mosaic one (as his gematria-based epilogue on Genesis's opening Bereshit makes clear).

claims.text: Allen says Ficino, drawn to man's standing on the middle rung, worked with a pentadic scheme of hypostases inherited from Proclus, the One, Mind, Soul, Quality and Body, in which Soul mediates between Mind and the corporeal.

quotes.text: The trope of the human microcosm haunted Ficino too, though he was most drawn to the image of man's standing on the middle rung of the cosmic ladder, for insofar as man is soul, he is a participant in the realm or hypostasis of Soul, which is the middle and therefore mediating hypostasis in the pentadic scheme of hypostases Ficino inherited from Proclus and the late ancient Neoplatonic tradition, the scheme of the One, Mind, Soul, Quality, and Body (i.e., matter in extension).

bears_on.note: Ficino's pentadic hypostases, against Pico's angelic-Mind emphasis.

judged.justification: Contrasts Ficino's pentad with Pico's Angel-centred scheme.

claims.text: Allen says Ficino's emphasis on Soul directs attention to life and the whole reflected in the part, whereas Pico's Platonic anthropocentrism and Genesis commitment underscore the uniqueness of man, of man in Christ and of Christ as the Idea of Man.

quotes.text: Ficino's emphasis on Soul and thus on the World Soul directs our attention away from the notion of particular entities and species toward the general concepts of life, of potentiality, of being, and specifically of being part of a greater whole while reflecting the whole in the part which is ourselves. Pico's Platonic anthropocentrism by contrast, along with his commitment to the Genesis myths of man's creation, serves in a way to underscore the uniqueness of man, and certainly of man in Christ and of Christ as the Idea of Man

bears_on.note: Allen's contrast: Ficino's World-Soul unity against Pico's Christological anthropocentrism.

quotes.text: Ficino's vision may be in a way more unitary, more panentheistic, since his metaphysics is attuned to his abiding fascination with harmony, with the antiphonal and responsive play of voices in the choir of creation, with the counterturns of the cosmic dance, and it looks, as we still do, to mathematics and particularly to the key notions of ratio and proportion

bears_on.note: Ficino's more unitary vision, by contrast with Pico.

claims.text: Allen says Pico's speculations on the principles of the emanative process are rich but not internally consistent, and that many of his problems are intrinsic to Neoplatonism and to Plotinus's attempts to probe the first flowing out of the One.

quotes.text: Pico's contribution, however, is interesting for different reasons. He has given us a rich, if not an internally consistent, set of speculations concerning the principles of the emanative process itself: the principles that underlie the birth of thought, of the world, of beauty, of love, of humanity, of Adam, of ourselves as particular beings, of ourselves in Christ as the Son of Man, and of God. Many of the problems that he encountered and that prevented him from arriving at consistency are demonstrably intrinsic to Neoplatonism itself and to Plotinus's iterated attempts to probe not so much into the genesis moment as into the emanative moment: the first flowing out of the One

bears_on.note: Allen's overall assessment of Pico's Neoplatonic speculations against the Ficinian achievement.

judged.justification: Diagnoses Pico's inconsistencies as intrinsic to Neoplatonic emanation.

claims.text: Allen argues that for Pico and Ficino the fascination with the origin of existence is the fundamental allure of Plotinian Platonism, and concludes that Pico should still be thought of as Ficino's fellow Neoplatonist, who joined him, however contentiously, in celebrating the birthday of Venus.

quotes.text: This fascination with the origin of existence, with the origin of the very thought of what does not yet exist in thought, constitutes for Pico and Ficino, I would argue, the fundamental allure of Plotinian Platonism.

In this important regard at least, we should continue to think of him as Ficino's fellow Neoplatonist, however Aristotelian or eclectic he may have been in many other respects; certainly he joined his older friend, however contentiously, in celebrating philosophically the birthday of Venus.

bears_on.note: Allen's concluding judgement: Pico remains Ficino's fellow Neoplatonist despite contentious disagreement.

judged.justification: Frames the Pico-Ficino disagreement as intra-Platonic.
